classification.tone: Gritty, operatic, mournful, and morally charged

evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving Catholic brother hunts the crime family that destroyed his home, while his cop sister races to stop him before vengeance and faith collide in a blood-soaked reckoning.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clear emotional engine — family annihilation, revenge, and moral reckoning — that is easy to grasp and easy to sell. The Catholic framework and crime-family structure give it a defined audience lane, though the intensity and specificity make it more targeted than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening massacre, the time jump, and the brother-sister split establish the story engine quickly and cleanly. The script keeps the central question legible: will Jacob’s grief-driven pursuit of justice consume him before Jodie can pull him back?

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie both have strong emotional traction, and Ethan adds a compelling moral counterweight. The supporting family members are vivid in function, though the story is most magnetic when it stays locked on the sibling triangle and Victor’s pressure on it.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Catholic ritual, confession structure, and repeated liturgical imagery give the script a distinct identity beyond a standard revenge thriller. The choice to frame violence through prayer, penance, and sacrament is confident and memorable.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with strong forward drive through the massacre, investigation, retaliation, and final confrontation. The escalation is clear and the set pieces keep arriving with purpose, especially once Jacob and Jodie start converging on the same target.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A Catholic revenge thriller centered on confession, absolution, and inherited violence feels fresh and immediately ownable. The script’s best idea is that justice here is not just legal or emotional — it is spiritual, and every major choice is measured against that.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The police station, church, mansion, docks, club, and graveyard all feel like parts of one social ecosystem, not random backdrops. The Risaldi family hierarchy, the city politics, and the church’s role in the aftermath create a world with visible pressure lines.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakably solemn but not inert: it mixes devotional language, family intimacy, and brutal criminal violence in a way that feels authored. The repeated hymns, confessions, and public rituals give the piece a signature emotional register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the revenge plot is a deeper argument about guilt, grace, inherited sin, and whether violence can ever be converted into meaning. The final church and confession material suggests a story that wants to be about salvation as much as punishment.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Jacob-Jodie-Ethan triangle carries real dramatic electricity, and Victor’s family system generates strong internal pressure. The ensemble is most effective when the family relationships are in conflict, because nearly every scene can turn on loyalty, shame, or protection.

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with several key exterior sequences
notable_requirements: Club with private decks and maintenance room

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical storytelling with some fire/smoke, blood, and a few stylized memory/vision transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, blood effects, fire, smoke, body impacts, and practical violence beats.

rights_flags.detail: Come Back by The Five Stairsteps, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, O Holy Night, Petals by Hole, 500 Miles by Peter, Paul and Mary, Good Looking by Suki Waterhouse, Clair de Lune, and L’Amour Toujours are all referenced or used as story texture.
311 is referenced in the radio announcement.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Premium streaming or prestige theatrical indie
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform or limited theatrical-to-streaming potential

cost.note: The footprint is mostly contained, but the club, docks, mansion, church, snow, fire, and multiple violence scenes push it above a microbudget lane.

cast.note: The script needs a strong four-lead core plus a sizable supporting family and law-enforcement ensemble, with child casting for Marcus and Jay.

location.note: It spans several distinct interiors and exteriors, including a mansion, docks, club, church, graveyard, and snowbound roads.

content.note: The script includes child murder, executions, gun violence, bloodshed, grief, and sexual assault testimony, which narrows platform and rating options.

rights.note: Multiple named songs and a branded antidepressant are embedded in the script and would need clearance planning.

strengths.what_it_means: The Catholic framework gives the movie a built-in thematic spine that elevates it beyond a standard revenge thriller and makes the emotional stakes legible in every scene. Prestige buyers and faith-adjacent audiences alike will respond to a crime story that treats confession, absolution, and grace as active dramatic forces.
strengths.evidence: Confession booth scenes, adoration chapel scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and Jacob’s repeated Act of Contrition structure the climax and aftermath.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The sibling triangle carries the movie.
strengths.what_it_means: Jacob, Jodie, and Ethan create a three-way emotional engine that can anchor the whole film and give the cast real awards-bait material. Buyers looking for actor-forward crime drama will see a central relationship web that can hold the audience even when the plot turns operatic.
strengths.evidence: Jodie trying to stop Jacob, Ethan trying to redirect both of them, and the final ballroom confrontation where all three collide.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Victor is a formidable family tyrant.
strengths.what_it_means: Victor gives the film a clear, cinematic antagonist whose power comes from psychological dominance as much as violence, which is exactly the kind of role that attracts prestige character actors. The script gives him speeches, ritualized cruelty, and a final confrontation that can sell the movie on performance alone.
strengths.evidence: The ballroom photo-ripping sequence, his treatment of Alicia and the sons, and the final ballroom monologue about authority and sacrifice.

strengths.what_it_means: The recurring hymns, prayers, stained glass, confession, and sacramental language create a visual and sonic identity that can make the film feel authored and trailer-friendly. That kind of signature texture helps a buyer position the movie as more than a generic crime piece.
strengths.evidence: Come Back, O Holy Night, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, Clair de Lune, the confession booth, and the church service montage.

strengths.what_it_means: Police, city hall, the church, and the criminal family all operate as competing systems, which gives the story a broader social canvas than a simple home-invasion revenge setup. That makes the project feel scalable and gives producers multiple marketing hooks: crime, faith, civic collapse, and family tragedy.
strengths.evidence: Mayor Adams’ press conferences, the docks raid, the church vandalism, and the police briefing rooms.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on grace, not just blood.
strengths.what_it_means: The final movement turns the movie from a revenge engine into a redemption story, which broadens its emotional aftertaste and gives the ending a more lasting resonance. That’s the kind of close that can help a film travel with critics, festivals, and adult audiences who want catharsis with a moral argument.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s confession, Jodie and Marcus at the table, Father Michael’s closing prayer, and the empty-space montage.

whats_special.headline: RISALDI is a prestige-leaning crime thriller with a clear commercial spine: a Catholic family tragedy that turns revenge into confession and guilt into action. It offers a strong actor package, a memorable antagonist, and a tonal identity that feels built for festival attention and adult audience word-of-mouth.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 30s to early 40s · Catholic father/brother
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is a devastated, devout family man whose grief curdles into purpose. He’s tender with his family, volatile under pressure, and spiritually literate enough to know exactly how far he’s fallen even as he keeps walking toward it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea — a man whose pain is so internalized it becomes behavior, not speeches, until the pressure finally breaks him open. Actors who want a grief role with moral contradiction, physical intensity, and a final descent into violence will chase this hard.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late 30s to early 40s · police officer
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is a workaholic cop who uses motion, duty, and competence to outrun grief. She’s tough, defensive, and deeply loving, with the kind of emotional restraint that makes every crack in her armor count.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Amy Adams in Sharp Objects — a woman whose professionalism is also her coping mechanism, and whose unraveling is as compelling as her control. Strong dramatic leads looking for a role that can play authority, sisterhood, and emotional collapse in the same frame will want it.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 20s · morally conflicted family member
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the conscience inside a violent dynasty, a man who keeps trying to choose principle without fully knowing how to survive it. He’s anxious, articulate, and spiritually searching, which makes him the story’s most fragile and surprising moral center.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Paul Dano in There Will Be Blood and Jesse Plemons in The Master their most unsettling power — a soft-spoken man whose inner life keeps widening the frame. Actors who specialize in intelligence, shame, and quiet volatility will see a lot to play here.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Victor is a cold, theatrical patriarch who treats his family like a doctrine and his violence like discipline. He’s composed, cruel, and almost priest-like in the way he weaponizes shame, making him both a mob boss and a false god.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of commanding villain role that gave Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad and Michael Stuhlbarg in Boardwalk Empire their authority — a man whose intelligence makes the cruelty sharper. Veteran actors who want a monologue-rich, scene-dominating part with real moral weight will line up for it.

lead_characters.name: Katherine Smith
lead_characters.hook: Katherine is the emotional center of the Smith home, warm, practical, and quietly funny. Even in limited screen time, she reads as the kind of mother whose steadiness makes the loss of the family feel catastrophic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of maternal showcase that gave Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April and Melissa Leo in Frozen River their lived-in authority. Character actresses who can make a few scenes feel like the emotional architecture of the film will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Martin is a sadistic performer who seems to enjoy cruelty as much as control. He’s volatile, theatrical, and deeply damaged, with a childlike need for approval buried inside the brutality.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, prestige-villain territory that gave Jack Gleeson in Game of Thrones and Jesse Plemons in Civil War their unnerving charge — a character who can swing from wounded to monstrous in a beat. Actors who want a role with volatility, menace, and a chance to make the audience flinch will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 20s to early 30s · family enforcer
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the quieter brother, the one who still has enough humanity left to hesitate. He reads as loyal, frightened, and increasingly trapped, which gives him a tragic edge inside the family machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of doomed supporting role that gave Michael Pitt in Boardwalk Empire and Shea Whigham in True Detective their texture — a man whose fear is always just beneath the surface. Actors who like playing loyalty under pressure will find a lot of playable tension here.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument, a mountain of muscle who carries out orders with brutal calm. He’s less verbal than the others, which makes his violence feel even more chilling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of silent-enforcer role that gives actors the chance to build menace through presence, not dialogue — the territory of Tom Hardy in Bronson or Dave Bautista in smaller, moodier work. Physical performers who can communicate threat with stillness will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Tyler Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Tyler is a taunting, sadistic brother who uses cruelty as sport. He’s the family’s most openly vicious presence, and his glee makes him especially memorable in the violence scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of nasty, scene-stealing supporting role that lets an actor go full predator for a few high-impact sequences, like Walton Goggins in Justified or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom. Character actors who love a sharp, dangerous edge will want it.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Female · mid 50s · Victor’s wife, former stripper
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is a woman who has survived by shrinking herself inside a violent household. She carries humiliation, fear, and a buried maternal instinct, which makes her final scenes especially tragic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised, emotionally loaded supporting role that gave Jennifer Jason Leigh in The Hateful Eight and Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects such force. Actresses who can play submission, terror, and buried dignity in the same scene will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the family’s so-called pure one, a child trapped inside a violent dynasty and treated like a symbol more than a son. His silence and fear give the story its most painful innocence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that can become unforgettable with the right young performer, the emotional function of the boy in The Road or the child in Room. Casting directors will look for a kid who can hold stillness, fear, and vulnerability without overplaying it.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is compassionate, wise, and slyly funny, a priest who understands both doctrine and human weakness. He functions as the film’s moral interpreter without ever becoming abstract.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran character actor the warmth and authority of Paul Dano’s priestly counterweight in There Will Be Blood or Mark Margolis-style gravitas in a more humane register. Actors who can make exposition feel like counsel will want it.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Owens
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Owens is calm, professional, and trying to reach a man who no longer trusts language. She’s the film’s secular care figure, and her scenes help define Jacob’s emotional isolation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained but meaningful professional role that gives an actor the chance to play empathy under pressure, like the therapist figures in Ordinary People or Manchester by the Sea. Character actresses who can make one room feel emotionally consequential will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Chief Pitts
lead_characters.hook: Chief Pitts is a weary institutional figure trying to manage catastrophe without pretending he can fix it. He’s pragmatic, apologetic, and visibly burdened by the city’s failures.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of law-enforcement authority role that gives an actor the grounded gravitas of Jeffrey Wright in a procedural or John Carroll Lynch in a prestige drama. Performers who can make bureaucracy feel human will respond to it.

lead_characters.name: Captain Ricks
lead_characters.hook: Captain Ricks is the hard-edged face of the investigation, a man who knows the city’s ugliness and keeps moving anyway. He’s less emotionally open than Pitts, which gives the police side of the story a sharper institutional texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of procedural authority role that gives an actor the clipped intensity of Michael Kelly in House of Cards or Shea Whigham in a crime drama. Actors who can play pressure without melodrama will fit it well.

lead_characters.name: Mayor Adams
lead_characters.hook: Mayor Adams is polished, performative, and opportunistic, the kind of civic leader who can turn tragedy into a podium moment. He gives the film a public-facing hypocrisy that contrasts with the private violence of the Risaldis.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of political role that lets an actor play charm, damage control, and self-preservation in one package, the territory of actors like Michael Shannon in smaller political turns or Paul Sparks in prestige drama. Performers who enjoy playing public masks will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Officer Daniels
lead_characters.hook: Officer Daniels is the steady working cop who keeps trying to pull Jodie back from the edge. He’s functional, grounded, and useful as a human counterweight in the police material.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of reliable supporting role that gives an actor the grounded utility of a Michael Cudlitz or David Harbour type in a crime ensemble. Actors who can make a few scenes feel lived-in and protective will want it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a crime thriller that plays like a moral reckoning.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two features, especially those who already work in performance-forward drama or spiritually inflected genre. This material rewards restraint, ritual, and actor-driven escalation more than flashy plotting.
director_appeal.detail: The film gives a director a chance to stage violence as consequence, not spectacle, and to use church, confession, and family interiors as dramatic architecture. It will appeal to filmmakers who like tonal control, strong blocking, and scenes where silence carries as much weight as dialogue.

buyer_appeal.lane: Prestige crime thriller / faith-adjacent adult drama
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be packaged around one strong lead, one strong antagonist, and a credible supporting ensemble rather than a full name-talent stack. The contained interiors, repeatable locations, and adult thematic lane make it viable for festival-to-platform or limited theatrical buyers looking for elevated genre with a clear hook.

considerations.area: The opening massacre is the engine.
considerations.detail: The prologue is unforgettable and does the heavy lifting of the premise, but it is also carrying the emotional and narrative load for the first act. One lever would be to seed a little more of Jacob and Jodie’s present-day relationship before the massacre lands, so the loss hits with even more personal force once the story jumps forward.

considerations.area: The middle can keep tightening around Jacob.
considerations.detail: The church, police, and Risaldi material all works, but the script is most electric when Jacob’s choices are forcing the next turn. A next pass could consider trimming any stretch where the investigation explains the world more than Jacob’s obsession changes it, so the momentum stays locked to his descent.

considerations.area: The Risaldi family tree is dense.
considerations.detail: The family hierarchy is vivid, but there are a lot of named players moving through the same pressure system. If the goal is to protect clarity and production efficiency, one simplification lever would be to collapse any functionally similar family roles so the audience tracks the power structure instantly and the shoot footprint stays leaner.

The script uses several named songs as emotional markers, and those choices are doing real atmospheric work. A producer pass should preserve the musical identity while planning early for clearance or alternate needle-drop options so the final cut can keep the same emotional architecture.

considerations.area: Jodie’s final turn is a strong anchor.
considerations.detail: Her confrontation with Jacob at the end lands because she is no longer just the cop or the sister — she becomes the person asking him to survive himself. A next pass could continue foregrounding that dual identity earlier in the script, so her authority in the climax feels inevitable rather than reserved for the final stretch.

The confession booth and Father Michael scenes are some of the script’s most distinctive pages, because they turn theology into drama instead of commentary. The version of the movie that keeps those scenes concise and emotionally pointed will preserve the film’s signature while avoiding any sense of sermonizing.
